title: Turning Direction into Delivered Work
author: Ian Hallett
summary: Ian Hallett asks what happens to a decision between the moment it is made and the moment it is supposed to take effect. His argument is that when agreed work is not done, the cause is usually not the team's discipline but three things the leader does afterwards: making clear what is expected, following up on whether it happened, and putting time, people and money behind it. He cites Judge and Piccolo's meta-analysis, in which contingent reward predicted results almost as well as transformational leadership, and Locke and Latham's goal-setting research on specific, difficult goals. The Intel story, drawn from Burgelman's study, shows middle managers moving capacity to microprocessors before the stated strategy changed. Hallett turns this into three handovers to check, each with a concrete test and wording a leader can use. He closes with honest limits, noting that the arrangement is untested and the evidence on prioritisation is the thinnest.
points: Follow-up after a decision counts almost as much as inspiration during it, according to the pooled research on contingent reward and transformational leadership.

A team always executes something each week, so the real question is whether it matches what the leader said, as Intel's managers showed by funding microprocessors while the strategy still said memory chips.
The three handovers are from the leader to people three layers down, from the decision to a named owner with a date, and from the announcement to whoever controls time, people and money.
A simple audit of calendar hours against the stated top priority exposes the gap between words and spending.
Execution is not supervision when owners keep the record and the leader reads it, and bad news must be made safe to report.
quotes: Your team is executing something every week. The question is whether it is what you said.
When a leader announces one priority and funds another, people believe the funding.
Before any decision is made, every action agreed in it needs one named owner and a date.
A status report is worth little until bad news is safe to put on it, so the first time someone reports red, thank them in front of the others.
If the top priority received the fewest hours, you have found the gap. Then move hours to it, or change the ranking.
Supervision means the team has to ask you where things stand. In the handovers above, the owners keep the record, and you read it, and the team can see its own progress.
Put one question to your leadership team at its next meeting: “If someone read our calendars and budgets for last month, what would they say our top priority was?
